item.title: Senators back plan to cultivate embryos for scientific research
item.description:
Senators back plan to cultivate embryos for scientific research

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch senate has approved plans to allow specially grown embryos to be used for research into hereditary illnesses and infertility.

The bill, proposed by the liberal parties VVD and D66 during the last cabinet term while D66 was in opposition, achieved a narrow majority of 38 to 35 votes in the upper house.

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP are opposed to cultivating embryos for scientific research because they see it as a violation of the sanctity of life.

The far-right PVV also voted against the plan, which party senator Ilse Bezaan called a “morally reprehensible” measure. “There are good alternatives, we shouldn’t open the door to a sliding scale,” she said.

Until now only embryos that are discarded during IVF treatment could be used for research purposes, but scientists say that using newly fertilised embryos would allow them to study the effect of treatments in the early stages of development.

item.title: Meat sector and government put profits before welfare: report
item.description:
Meat sector and government put profits before welfare: report

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch meat industry and the government are both failing to protect animal welfare, and put profits first as the laws are vague and hard to enforce.

“The system is failing to protect animal welfare: the government and the sector are falling short,” the committee, chaired by former transport inspectorate chief Jan van den Bos, said in its final report.

The agriculture ministry set up the panel in 2024 to review oversight of the meat chain. It found that food safety and animal health are well protected.

Welfare is harmed on a large scale even when companies follow the law, the committee said, because legal standards are vague and current production methods and costs are always the starting point when they are set.

Some 535 million animals are slaughtered in the Netherlands every year, more than 518 million of them chickens. Inspection figures cited in the report show that around 3 million birds arrive at slaughterhouses injured each year.

Two-thirds of 170 pig farms checked in 2023 and 2024 by the food and product safety watchdog NVWA were breaking welfare rules. The watchdog spends just 8% of its capacity on animal welfare.

The committee said the agriculture minister gives the sector too little direction and repeatedly delays decisions.

item.title: “Very dangerous”: Rights group condemns Kristallnacht speech
item.description:
“Very dangerous”: Rights group condemns Kristallnacht speech

November 10, 2026 Louis Gore-Langton

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Kristallnacht remembrance service in Amsterdam’s Portuguese Synagogue has stirred controversy after the keynote speaker condemned the Red Line protests and said labelling the Gaza war a genocide was rooted in anti-Semitism.

In a highly political speech, Chanan Hertzberger, chair of Jewish umbrella organisation CJO, denounced the “genocide lie” in front of a congregation containing senior cabinet members including the prime minister Rob Jetten, who also spoke.

Gerard Jonkman, director of Amsterdam-based Rights Forum, which campaigns on behalf of Palestinian rights, told Dutch News Hertzberger’s speech was “absolutely unacceptable”.

“This is also mixing the issue of anti-Semitism with criticism of Israel,” he said, “which is very, very, very dangerous.”

Hertzberger began his speech by thanking Jetten for not giving in to “the demands of the organisers of yesterday’s anti-Israel demonstration”, which he said amounted “directly or indirectly” to wiping Israel off the map.

“Who is being held responsible, in Arnhem, in Groningen and in Amsterdam for this so-called genocide?” he said. “We, the Jews. In our own own cities. In our streets. In our children’s classrooms. We are being ostracised and pushed to the margins of society.”

Only hours before, Jetten had spoken to RTL Nieuws saying it had been “impossible to miss” the protest and that he decided to stay away (having attended previous ones) because of his new role as PM, which he and his fellow cabinet member have used from the beginning to “increase pressure on Israel”.

“He embarrassed Jetten”

Jonkman said he thought Hertzberger had embarrassed Jetten and that the prime minister should now react to “these ridiculous accusations of hatred towards Israel.”

He said many Jewish people joined Sunday’s demonstration, among them Holocaust survivors and children of Holocaust survivors, and that many people he had spoken to were hurt by the speech.

Linking the protest to anti-Semitism in this way makes Jewish people in the Netherlands appear accountable for the policies of the Israeli government, he said.

Hertzberger said the “lie” that Israel was committing genocide now “marches weekly through our streets”, citing chants at Sunday’s protest, though he added that not all demonstrators were anti-Semites.

Zionism

He claimed that in fact the majority of Jewish people in the Netherlands are Zionists, that Zionism is the recognition of Israel’s right to exist as a “safe, independent Jewish state”, and that those things are now “more important than ever”.

He mentioned the numerous attacks on Jewish schools and synagogues in the Netherlands this year, and said that the images of Gaza left no one unmoved, including himself.

A United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects.

The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both men have firmly denied the allegations.

The CJO has not yet replied for comment.

Jetten’s premiership has marked a downturn in Dutch-Israeli relations. Since the cabinet enacted a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories in September, Israel has responded by stripping Dutch diplomats of their status and removing Dutch officials from a US-backed Gaza ceasefire centre.

item.title: Village threatened by port expansion could be saved by new plan
item.description:
Village threatened by port expansion could be saved by new plan

November 10, 2026 Gordon Darroch

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A village with 1,100 inhabitants that has been facing shutdown for the last year under plans to expand an industrial port in Noord-Brabant could be saved after the government came up with an alternative, smaller-scale development.

The municipal council in Moerdijk said a year ago that the entire village would have to be demolished to make room for the Powerport development, which needs 400 to 500 hectares of land.

The expansion of the port and industrial site includes high-voltage substations, transformer stations, and pipelines to support the transition to clean energy and supply power to homes and businesses in the coming decades.

But junior climate minister Jo-Annes de Bat said in a letter to parliament on Tuesday that “a new scenario has arisen” that would involve a smaller expansion of around 200 hectares, allowing Moerdijk to remain.

Pim Meijer, spokesman for community group Dorpstafel Moerdijk, gave a cautious welcome to the new plan, but said the uncertainty surrounding the village’s future had taken its toll.

“People have no perspective,” he told Dutch News. “They’re suffering from stress and physical ailments. This year 25 people have already signed up for the scheme that lets them sell their house to the council and that’s a direct result of the uncertainty.”

Quality of life

He said villagers wanted the council, the province and the municipality to set down clear parameters to guarantee the village’s future and quality of life.

“What people don’t want is to see the industrial zone constantly encroaching on the village, which is what’s been going on for years. We want to draw a boundary and say: thus far and no further,” he said.

“If people with children leave that has an impact on our primary schools and our social clubs, and if no houses are built then new people can’t come to live in Moerdijk. But as long as people believe in a future for Moerdijk we will keep fighting for it.”

The government will continue to honour its financial commitments to Moerdijk, including a pledge to fully compensate villagers for their land and property and €25 million in community funding.

De Bat said the amount of space required for the development was less than previously estimated, partly because more efficient batteries were available and the government has downscaled its ambitions to develop hydrogen power.

“Residents of the village of Moerdijk and the surrounding region have rightly been asking for clarity for a long time,” he wrote.

item.title: Toolkit to help teachers spot suspected child abuse goes live
item.description:
Toolkit to help teachers spot suspected child abuse goes live

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Schools have started using a new digital support package to help teachers alert the authorities to cases of suspected domestic abuse and neglect.

The toolkit has been developed to try to increase the number of reports from schools, which is lower in the Netherlands than in neighbouring countries.

It is the product of two years of research that began when a series of cases came to light in which children had been systematically abused and tortured by their families. The children attended school but teachers were either unaware of the problems at home or unwilling to intervene.

Since 2019 teachers have been required to pass on details of children who they suspect of being abused to Veilig Thuis, the agency that specialises in domestic abuse and can compel parents to accept help.

The education minister at the time, Hugo de Jonge, said on average every classroom contained one child who was a victim of abuse or neglect at home.

The number of reports schools has almost doubled in the last seven years to around 4,000, while Veilig Thuis has advised in more than 9,500 other cases.

Need for training

But experts warn that teachers still lack the necessary expertise and are reluctant to contact the authorities because they fear repercussions from parents.

Carlijn van Baak, a researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement who helped develop the toolkit, told NOS: “Teachers don’t receive training in recognising the signs of child abuse as standard, but in practice it is very difficult because it’s not always obvious.”

She said teachers often had suspicions of abuse but were unsure of how to deal with it. “They try to organise help for the family, but it is often unclear what exactly is going on and when they should make a report.”

Veilig Thuis has also warned it is at the limits of its capacity to investigate abuse cases. Last year it dealt with 136,000 cases, two-thirds of which involved families who were previously unknown to the agency.

“At the moment we can’t guarantee that we can respond to every alert about safety in time,” Ida Ouweneel, a manager at Veilig Thuis’s national network, told NOS last month. “That’s very concerning for us.”

item.title: International student numbers rise as people leave US
item.description:
International student numbers rise as people leave US

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More international students are coming to study at Dutch universities, partly driven by people choosing to leave the US amid the current political climate, according to broadcaster NOS.

Around 17,600 first-year students this academic year come from abroad, up about 6% on last year, according to provisional figures from the university association UNL and the association of universities of applied sciences (VH), news agency ANP reported.

Universities had agreed to admit no more than 16,766 new international students a year, so that internationalisation would not come at the expense of Dutch students or undermine the Dutch language.

The universities say foreign students are “more often choosing to study in Europe because of developments in the United States”.

NOS linked this to president Donald Trump, who has tightened visa checks, clashed openly with several universities and interfered with academic freedom since returning to the White House.

UNL said the rise in foreign students was good news in itself, because they mainly study technical subjects in a sector short of staff. “We badly need international talent, particularly in priority sectors such as technology,” UNL chair Caspar van den Berg said, according to NOS.

“At the same time, universities have agreed to cap international intake. That is why we are taking targeted extra measures.”

Several universities will cut the number of places on English-taught psychology, economics, business administration and political science courses so that they stay below the agreed maximum next year. National student union ISO said it opposes caps on places and that every student should be free to choose their course.

item.title: Cabinet hopeful of securing majority for capital gains tax plan
item.description:
Cabinet hopeful of securing majority for capital gains tax plan

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The cabinet’s plans to introduce a capital gains tax are on course to clear both houses of parliament after three right-wing opposition parties signalled they were prepared to back the measure.

Junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg said in a debate on Monday that the trio of JA21, BBB and SGP would support the plan, overcoming objections from other opposition parties and criticism by the Council of State.

Coalition parties D66 and CDA also voiced reservations about the reform, with Henk-Jan Oosterhuis of D66 calling it a “rather creative explanation of the budget rules” and Christian Democrat Inge van Dijk admitting that it was “not pretty”.

Luc Stultiens, of the left-wing opposition party Pro, went further, accusing the coalition parties of writing “a blank cheque for €17 billion to the wealthy”, referring to the projected budget shortfall that will be created by the transition.

The three right-wing opposition parties would give the minority coalition a majority in the lower house, but the cabinet would still need to find support from one more party in the Senate.

€10 billion gap

The pensioners’ party 50Plus is seen as the most likely candidate, even though MP Corrie van Brenk said the “signal is red” during Monday’s debate. Oosterhuis pointed out that the latest revision is almost identical to a plan 50Plus tabled previously in the upper house.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen’s reform would replace the current system of taxing investments and savings annually, based on estimated rates of return, with a tax levied when assets are sold.

The finance ministry has estimated that the switch to capital gains tax will leave a €10 billion gap in the short term because investors will no longer pay tax on their assets every year.

The Box 3 levy was struck out in 2021 when the Supreme Court ruled that the use of fictional interest rates was deemed to breach European law.

The government introduced a stopgap measure allowing taxpayers to challenge their tax bill by submitting their actual financial results, but this is costing the treasury an estimated €3.5 billion a year.

The Council of State, which advises the cabinet on the legal implications of its bills, said Heinen’s plans to start charging tax on capital gains from 2028 were too hasty and would cause administrative problems at the tax office. Heinen compromised by shifting the start date for the new tax to 2029, which will increase the budget shortfall.

item.title: National weather warnings over thick fog, Friesland car crash
item.description:
National weather warnings over thick fog, Friesland car crash

November 10, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Thick fog covered almost all of the Netherlands on Tuesday morning, cutting visibility to less than 20 metres in some places and causing long tailbacks and a head-on crash in Friesland.

The national weather service KNMI issued a code yellow warning for the whole country except Zeeland, the Wadden Islands, the IJsselmeer and Wadden Sea areas and parts of Limburg. The warning runs from 11.30pm on Monday until midday on Tuesday.

Around 6.50am, visibility in Flevoland had fallen below 20 metres, and 70 metres was recorded in Zuid-Holland, broadcaster NOS reported.

In Friesland, two cars collided on the N359 road between Koudum and Hemelum in dense fog, regional news site Omrop Fryslân reported. Ambulances were called to the scene in around 6.50am; how many were injured is not yet known.

The KNMI is advising drivers to slow down and leave more space. Front fog lights should go on when visibility is below 200 metres, and rear fog lights below 50 metres.

Fog may hang over the north all day and come back on Tuesday night. Rain is forecast for Wednesday morning’s rush hour in the centre and south.

item.title: Jetten says it is “not his place” to join Gaza demonstration
item.description:
Jetten says it is “not his place” to join Gaza demonstration

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has defended his decision to stay away from last weekend’s mass demonstration in Amsterdam against Israel’s war in Gaza.

Organisers claimed around 200,000 people joined the Red Line rally, the fourth to be held since Israel began its bombing campaign and ground offensive in response to the attacks by Hamas in October 2023.

Jetten took part in a similar demonstration in Amsterdam in October last year as leader of the D66 party, which was then in opposition, but said it was “not his place” to attend as prime minister. He also declined to describe Israel’s offensive as a genocide, as he did a year ago.

“Hundreds of thousands of people in the Netherlands took to the streets because they are concerned about the terrible humanitarian situation of many Palestinians,” he said.

“That’s why the cabinet has pledged from the outset to offer more help and put pressure on Israel.”

But he added: “I don’t think it’s my place at all to be at a demonstration like this. People have shown how moved they are by the situation of millions of Palestinians and at the same time they have urged the cabinet to act.”

VVD blockade

The prime minister has come under pressure from human rights organisations to speak out against Israel, but his coalition includes the right-wing liberal VVD party, whose leadership is staunchly pro-Israeli.

Jetten insisted at his weekly press conference on Friday that the Dutch government had made clear during bilateral talks with Israel that “the situation in Gaza, the West Bank, but also in Jordan and Syria is unacceptable”.

But he ruled out taking stronger measures such as an arms embargo or declaring that Israel was committing “genocide and ethnic cleansing against Palestinians”, as the protest organisers demanded.

Senior politicians including Amsterdam’s former Labour party (PvdA) mayor Job Cohen have also criticised Jetten’s leadership on the issue.

Cohen and former VVD foreign affairs minister, Jozias van Aartsen, who are both Jewish, said in an interview with the Volkskrant at the weekend that they were joining the demonstration to protest against Israel’s actions.

Humanitarian values

Cohen told TV talks show Pauw, De Wit and Moggré: “I have had doubts in the past, specifically about the term genocide, because I found it so incredibly difficult to apply it not to Israel, but to this Israeli government.

“I think it’s extremely important that Israel exists as a place of refuge where Jews can go, but I think this government is appalling. My feeling is that it’s almost impossible to deny anymore that what is happening, to an increasing degree, has elements of genocide.”

Van Aartsen was critical of his own party for refusing to push for sanctions against Israel. “It would be fitting for a party that claims to be liberal to defend basic values such as humanity and international law, but they are standing by and watching,” he said.

item.title: Tilburg arms manufacturer buys rights to Israeli weapon designs
item.description:
Tilburg arms manufacturer buys rights to Israeli weapon designs

November 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Tilburg-based defence company AIA is buying technological data from Israeli arms manufacturer IWI, best known for the Uzi machine gun, and which is the main supplier of small arms for the Israeli military and police forces, broadcaster NOS reported.

AIA is specifically buying design information for two guns, noted for their ability to shoot down drones, the Arad 5 rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun.

AIA’s director Gerard Zondervan told NOS that “Europe is calling”, that the bloc needs to produce its own weapons, and that he would not discuss politically contentious issues regarding Israel such as the war on Gaza.

In January, MPs adopted a motion calling on the government to reduce the Netherlands’ reliance on Israeli weapons, citing concerns about war crimes. The motion says the Netherlands has bought €2 billion worth of equipment from Israeli defence firms in recent years.

The Netherlands has also blocked exports of F-35 fighter jet parts to Israel since an appeals court ruling in February 2024, and kept the ban in place after the Supreme Court overturned that ruling in October 2025.

Zondervan said AIA had had no contact with the Dutch government regarding the deal, and that production will begin in Tilburg and then move into an expanded facility in Overijssel.

The announcement comes shortly after the defence ministry launched the National Institute for Defence technology (NIDT), to speed up development and cooperation for the arms industry.

NIDT will get €350 million a year from 2028 onwards, intended to strengthen defences in the North Sea amid escalating conflict with Russia.
